questions.q: What does a p-value of 0.03 actually represent?
options: There is a 3% probability that the null hypothesis is true
There is a 3% probability of observing a test statistic at least as extreme as the one observed, assuming the null hypothesis is true
There is a 97% probability that the alternative hypothesis is true
The effect size is 0.03
questions.explain: A p-value is strictly a statement about the probability of the observed data (or more extreme) under the assumption that H₀ is true. It is not the probability that H₀ (or H₁) is true.

questions.q: A researcher rejects a null hypothesis that was, in fact, true. What is this an example of?
options: A Type II error
A Type I error
High statistical power
A one-sided test
questions.explain: Rejecting a true null hypothesis is a Type I error (a false positive), with probability equal to the chosen significance level α.

questions.q: Holding sample size fixed, if you lower the significance level α from 0.05 to 0.01 to reduce false positives, what typically happens to the Type II error rate β?
options: β decreases as well
β increases, since it becomes harder to reject H₀ even when it's false
β is unaffected by the choice of α
β becomes exactly zero
questions.explain: Lowering α makes the rejection threshold stricter, which reduces Type I errors but, holding sample size fixed, makes it harder to detect real effects — increasing Type II error (β) and reducing power (1 − β).

questions.q: In a one-sample t-test, what reference distribution does the test statistic t = (x̄ − μ₀)/(s/√n) follow under the null hypothesis?
options: A standard normal distribution, always
A Student's t-distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom
A Poisson distribution with rate n
A uniform distribution on [0, 1]
questions.explain: Because the population variance is unknown and estimated from the sample (via s), the test statistic follows a Student's t-distribution with n − 1 degrees of freedom, not a standard normal.

questions.q: A strategy has a genuinely small positive true mean daily return. A one-year backtest (n=252) fails to reject H0: mean=0 at the 5% level. What is the most likely explanation?
options: The true mean must actually be zero
The test has low statistical power to detect a small effect with only one year of noisy daily data
The t-test is invalid for financial returns
A Type I error has definitely occurred
questions.explain: Daily returns are noisy relative to a small true mean, and one year of data often provides insufficient statistical power to detect a small but real effect — a failure to reject H0 is not proof that H0 is true, just that the evidence wasn't strong enough to overcome the noise.
